To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

DTI of the pancreas using b-values of 0 and 500 s/mm2, and 100 and 500 s/ mm2, can characterize pancreatic tissue, and that the difference between these two sets of b-values can be used to differentiate healthy from cancerous pancreas.

DTI using b-values of 0,100 s/mm2 can characterize the water diffusion and perfusion of healthy pancreas tissue and that the reduction in the diffusion and perfusion parameters in PDACs, in comparison to healthy pancreas tissue, can be utilized to detect malignancy.

DTI of the pancreas can be performed using b-values of 0 and 500 s/mm2 to characterize healthy pancreatic tissue, taking into account the fast IVIM component, and that the presence of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma can be identified using a DTI protocol that includes b-values of 500 and 100 s/ mm2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing DTI protocols that can be used for the characterization of the pancreas tissue and for the detection of pancreatic malignancy.
the development of a novel MRI protocol for pancreatic tissue characterization, which is sensitive to the diffusion and perfusion changes in PDAC.
the development of a DTI protocol that enables characterization of the diffusion and anisotropic properties of healthy and malignant pancreatic tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) technique, as described in the present work, has the potential to be used as a complementary tool for pancreatic cancer imaging.
a DTI protocol with b-values of 0 and 500 s/mm2 is sensitive to the diffusion and perfusion changes associated with PDAC.

the DTI protocol presented herein, with the use of two reference b-values, 0 and 500 s/mm2, and the calculation of the diffusion parameters at these b-values, is useful in the characterization of pancreatic tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

DTI of the pancreas can be used as a non-invasive tool for characterizing pancreatic tissue, and that the combination of two b-values, 0 and 500 s/mm2 is sufficient to obtain a good characterization of the pancreatic tissue.
DTI of the pancreatic tissue using b-values of 0 and 500 s/mm2 is sensitive to the presence of PDAC.
DTI using two b-values, 0 and 500, is a promising tool for characterizing the pancreas.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a b-value of 100 s/mm² is sufficient for the characterization of pancreatic tissue diffusion properties, while a higher reference b-value is needed for the characterization of the diffusion properties in other abdominal tissues.
DTI of the pancreas can be performed with b-values of 0,100 s/mm2 to yield diffusion parameters that can help characterize normal pancreas and PDACs.
